Introduction and meaning
Hurt = bodily pain, disease or infirmity (old 319). Definition only; punishment is s. 115. BNS restatement of IPC 319. Cite the BNS number for facts on or after 1 July 2024.
In student language: BNS s. 114 is the rule on “Hurt”. The section provides that whoever causes bodily pain, disease or infirmity to any person is said to cause hurt. Do not stop at the heading. An examiner awards marks for the ingredients, the explanations and the illustrations, not for writing the title alone.

Why this is asked
Criminal law arguments turn on statutory ingredients. BNS s. 114 exists so that “Hurt” has a closed legal test in Chapter VI — Of Offences Affecting the Human Body. An authoritative analysis defines the concept, lists every ingredient, walks the statutory illustrations, states exceptions, and applies the test methodically to facts.
Chapter setting: Homicide, organised crime, terrorism, hurt, acid, restraint, assault, kidnapping and trafficking.

The provision in detail
114. Whoever causes bodily pain, disease or infirmity to any person is said to cause hurt

Essential ingredients
1. Whoever causes bodily pain, disease or infirmity to any person is said to cause hurt

examples.title: Example 1 — simple (teaching example)
examples.body: A short everyday fact pattern is tested against “Hurt”. Name BNS s. 114, list the ingredients, and say which facts match. This is a teaching example — the statute does not print a numbered illustration under this heading.

examples.title: Example 2 — practical application / distinction (teaching example)
examples.body: Change one ingredient so that BNS s. 114 fails. A complex problem or motion often hinges on this subtle missing ingredient. State the failure expressly. Label this as an example, never as a reported case.

hypotheticals.question: Whether BNS s. 114 (Hurt) applies, and how structured written arguments should be framed.
hypotheticals.analysis:
Step 1 — Identify the provision. The correct current-law cite is BNS s. 114 (Hurt), Chapter VI — Of Offences Affecting the Human Body.
Step 2 — State the legal test in your own words, then list the ingredients:
   (1) Whoever causes bodily pain, disease or infirmity to any person is said to cause hurt
Step 3 — Check limitations, provisos and the rest of the Chapter so you do not apply s. 114 in a vacuum.
Step 4 — Map each fact to an ingredient. Write “this fact proves ingredient (a)” or “this fact is missing, so the section is not made out”.
Step 5 — Conclude. If every essential ingredient is proved and no exception covers the case, BNS s. 114 applies. If any essential ingredient fails, say so and stop. Do not invent a different section to save the answer.

misconceptions.trap: Copying a statutory illustration without mapping it to an ingredient.
misconceptions.correction: Quote the illustration, then write which ingredient it proves or which ingredient is missing. Mapping is the core evidentiary link.

questionsAndAnswers.question: Legal Assessment & Statutory Note: BNS s. 114 (Hurt)
questionsAndAnswers.answer:
Introduction. BNS s. 114 deals with Hurt. It sits in Chapter VI — Of Offences Affecting the Human Body of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023. After 1 July 2024 this is the current-law citation for this offence / definition / punishment.

Meaning. Hurt = bodily pain, disease or infirmity (old 319). Definition only; punishment is s. 115. BNS restatement of IPC 319. Cite the BNS number for facts on or after 1 July 2024.

Legal rule. In student language: BNS s. 114 is the rule on “Hurt”. The section provides that whoever causes bodily pain, disease or infirmity to any person is said to cause hurt. Do not stop at the heading. An examiner awards marks for the ingredients, the explanations and the illustrations, not for writing the title alone.

Essential ingredients. An authoritative analysis must list them, not hide them in one paragraph:
1. Whoever causes bodily pain, disease or infirmity to any person is said to cause hurt

Illustration. Give one short original example (label it as an example) and apply the ingredients.

Limitations. Apply only the conditions written in s. 114. Do not import a defence from a different chapter unless the question requires it.

Connected sections. Read with BNS s. 115, BNS s. 116. A preliminary brief mentions the neighbour; comprehensive submissions explain the exact distinction.

Conclusion. BNS s. 114 is the complete current-law heading for Hurt. Define, list ingredients, use an illustration, note any explanation or exception, apply, cite. That is a complete statutory structure.

Comprehensive Written Submissions. Deepen the doctrinal synthesis with four foundational layers.

Layer 1 — Place the section in the Chapter. Homicide, organised crime, terrorism, hurt, acid, restraint, assault, kidnapping and trafficking.. Show why this heading sits where it sits.

Layer 2 — Work a second, slightly harder hypothetical. Change one ingredient and show why the section then fails.

Layer 3 — Distinction. Contrast BNS s. 114 with BNS s. 115, BNS s. 116. Write a short table in prose: meaning, ingredients, stage of the case, consequence. Confusion of neighbouring sections is the most common reason arguments collapse under judicial scrutiny.



Layer 5 — Application and current-law close. Apply the test to the problem facts in IRAC form (Issue, Rule, Application, Conclusion). Close with: “The governing citation on or after 1 July 2024 is BNS s. 114.”
